specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** rider-elephant-path
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify nine change tactics as directing the rider, motivating the elephant, or shaping the path, correctly placing at least eight of nine on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** the Switch framework, direct the rider, motivate the elephant, shape the path, and the nine tactics (all defined in the section "The Switch Framework" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 9 tactics in one of three bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct part" column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Giving people information is always enough. (2) Emotion is an obstacle to change. (3) Changing the environment is not really leading. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying a tactic requires identifying whom it is aimed at: the thinking mind, the feeling mind, or the situation. Three tactics per part ensure the learner sees the full set and not one favorite. **Content:** Three bins with definitions on request: | Part | Definition shown | |---|---| | Direct the rider | Give the thinking mind clarity about what to do and where it leads | | Motivate the elephant | Engage feeling and identity so people want to act | | Shape the path | Change the situation so that the right behavior is easier | Nine tactics: | # | Tactic shown to the learner | Correct part | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Find the classroom where students like yours already thrive with the tool and copy what that teacher does. | Direct the rider | Following a bright spot gives clear, proven direction. | | 2 | Give teachers a one-page script for the first week: what to click and what to say on days one to five. | Direct the rider | Scripting the critical moves removes ambiguity. | | 3 | Show a vivid picture of the exhibition night that the freed afternoons will make possible. | Direct the rider | Pointing to the destination clarifies where the change leads. | | 4 | Share a story of a student's breakthrough so that teachers feel why this matters. | Motivate the elephant | Finding the feeling engages emotion. | | 5 | Ask each teacher to try one ten-minute activity this week. | Motivate the elephant | Shrinking the change makes it feel doable. | | 6 | Invite teachers to see themselves as learning coaches, not lecturers. | Motivate the elephant | Growing people's identity builds motivation. | | 7 | Fix the single sign-on so the login works on the first try. | Shape the path | Tweaking the environment removes friction. | | 8 | Add a standing fifteen-minute dashboard check to the weekly team meeting. | Shape the path | Building a habit makes the behavior routine. | | 9 | Make visible that most teachers in the neighboring school already use it. | Shape the path | Rallying the herd makes the behavior the norm. | **Provenance:** The framework follows Heath and Heath (2010), as described in the chapter. The tactics are illustrative, written for this chapter. **Rules:** Each tactic has exactly one correct part, given in Content, and each part has exactly three tactics. A tactic is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 9. Mastery is a score >= 8. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one tactic at a time and the three parts. 2. The learner places the tactic and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct part and reason are shown. 4. After all 9 tactics, the sim shows the score and the tactics grouped by part. 5. The learner should notice that three of the tactics change nothing about people and everything about the situation. **Feedback:** 9 tactics, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [part]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask whom the tactic is aimed at: the thinking mind, the feeling mind, or the situation. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the part]." After the second attempt the correct part is revealed and the tactic counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 9" is shown. Final message for a score >= 8: "You can tell which part of the change a tactic serves." For a score < 8: "Review the three parts and try again; the tactics will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Tactic 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three parts, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 9," and the prompt "Which part of the change does this tactic serve?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter names nine tactics, three per part, as in the table. The mastery bar is 8 of 9.
